A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across relocation and renumbering.

before.justification: v4 reports original function-approximation experiments in Tables 1–3 and Figures 7–8, along with pretraining ablations and an appendix learning-rate study.

after.justification: v5 retains those original experiments and adds concrete-strength regression, two-spiral classification, CIFAR-10, and ImageNet results in Appendices A.10–A.11.

M1.justification: The triangle-peak parameterization, scaling recurrence, and Algorithm 1 remain unchanged. Appendix A.10 adapts training to classification using cross entropy and implements the block-diagonal second-stage restriction previously suggested in v4 Section 5. These are limited adaptations of the existing method.

E1.justification: v5 retains the analytic function tasks and adds eight-feature concrete-strength regression, two-spiral classification, and CIFAR-10 and ImageNet classification. This substantially expands coverage beyond v4's one- and two-dimensional analytic examples.

E2.justification: The corresponding original comparisons retain Kaiming/default initialization and RAAI, with unchanged comparator membership. The new benchmarks also compare against Kaiming initialization; dense/block-diagonal and CNN configurations introduce experimental settings rather than another initialization method. Adding 'Kaiming' to the default-network labels clarifies an existing baseline.

E3.justification: The original one-dimensional protocols remain unchanged. New protocols include matched dense and block-diagonal comparisons, an epoch-500 parameterization switch, a three-convolution CIFAR-10 network, and ImageNet evaluation using frozen pretrained VGG16 convolutional weights with two epochs of classifier training.

E4.justification: Appendix A.10 adds a substantive test of whether maintaining block isolation during second-stage training preserves the method's benefits, using concrete regression and spiral classification. v4 suggested this remedy without evaluating it. The original pretraining, differentiability, structural-retention, and learning-rate analyses are retained.

E5.justification: The original minimum/mean summaries over 30 models and best-of-30 learning-rate analysis are unchanged. The added experiments introduce no stated repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 and retained experimental plots are unchanged, but Figures 15–18 add substantial results. Concrete test losses are 22.3 versus 21.2 for dense networks and 30.1 versus 40.8 for block-diagonal networks, proposed versus Kaiming. Spiral cross-entropy losses are 0.0032 versus 0.63; new image experiments also report lower losses. These are newly evaluated settings, not improvements to v4's existing scores.

T1.justification: v5 reformulates Theorem 3.1 around a continuous derivative and its derivative-series representation, explicitly restricts Theorem A.5 to bend points, and adds uniform-convergence and continuity reasoning. Appendix A.8 adds Zaslavsky's theorem and a derived region-count formula for groups of parallel hyperplanes. These substantially extend the mathematical treatment while retaining the scaling recurrence.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: exponential region counts through reparameterization, constrained pretraining, improved function approximation, and extensions to nonconvex and multidimensional functions. The added experiments support these existing claims without redefining the main contribution.

C2.justification: v5 substantially qualifies applicability: Appendix A.10 explains that dense implementations can tie or underperform ordinary networks, while preserving block structure can help under restricted parameter budgets. It adds switching-time and optimizer-state-reset limitations, including temporary loss spikes. Appendix A.11 explicitly distinguishes preliminary CNN benefits from the tightly controlled theoretical setting.

D1.justification: The new studies substantially expand technical documentation: depth-five blocks, 32/16 blocks with widths 128/64, the epoch-500 switch, frozen pretrained VGG16 convolutional weights, and image-learning rates of 0.001 and 0.00001. These additions describe new experimental implementations; they do not establish changes to the retained experiments.

R1.justification: v5 adds discussion of Chen and Ge's geometric parameterization, Elbrachter et al.'s conditioning analysis, and Eckle and Schmidt-Hieber's spline comparisons. Additional citations support expressivity metrics, reverse engineering, region counting, and the concrete dataset. These supplement the existing research positioning rather than replace it.

P1.justification: v5 locally revises related-work and proof exposition, shortens subsection headings, adds terminology explanations and appendix signposting, and removes the review-status header. The main six-section narrative and most existing prose remain intact; much of the expansion is new scientific content.

P2.justification: v5 redraws Figure 9, adds derivative and region-count illustrations in Figures 11 and 13, and adds four empirical displays in Figures 15–18. It also groups Tables 1–3 together and relocates existing figures. The old second-derivative illustration and learning-rate plot remain as Figures 12 and 14.

improvement.justification: v5 substantially improves support for, and qualification of, the proposed extensions. v4 offered only analytic one- and two-dimensional experiments; Appendices A.10–A.11 add practical evaluations and expose the important dense-versus-block-diagonal limitation. Expanded convergence, continuity, and region-count reasoning strengthens the theoretical account. The new empirical evidence remains preliminary because protocol details and uncertainty reporting are incomplete, but the gains in evidentiary support and understanding of applicability are substantial.
